chunk_findings.detail: `failed_over` deliberately returns `False` for an `UNAVAILABLE` result whose reason starts with `"the diff is empty"`, but `run_chain` uses `not failed_over(res)` as the test for “a reviewer answered.” Given a reviewer that returns `ReviewResult(status=UNAVAILABLE, reason="the diff is empty")`, `run_chain` returns an `Outcome` whose evidence contains `answered_by` and `answered_family` for that reviewer. That is wrong because the result is explicitly not a reviewer answer; the gate evidence falsely records an answer/family where there is none.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:run_chain

chunk_findings.detail: `run_chain` assumes `chain` is non-empty. If `chain` is empty, the loop never sets `last`, and the final `if last is None: first = chain[0]` raises `IndexError`. `order` can return an empty chain, for example when `[review].gate_order` names only unknown reviewers or a lane fallback has no models, so a configured typo can crash the gate instead of returning an unavailable `Outcome`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:run_chain

chunk_findings.detail: `_load` catches only `OSError`, `ValueError`, and `AttributeError`, but converts every JSON value with `float(v)`. If the cool-down file contains a JSON object with a non-numeric value such as `{"kimi": [300]}` or `{"kimi": null}`, `float(v)` raises `TypeError`, which propagates through `left`/`mark` and crashes `run_chain`, despite the class doc stating that unreadable cool-down data should mean no memory and no error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:CoolDowns._load

chunk_findings.detail: The docs state that a reviewer joins the chain when it is named in `[review].priority_default`, but in the same sentence say that `[review].gate_order` “replaces the default for that gate.” Given `[review].priority_default = ["gemini","kimi"]` and `[review].gate_order = {critic = "qwen,deepseek"}`, the docs simultaneously say `gemini` joins the `critic` chain because it is in `priority_default` and does not join it because `gate_order` replaces the default. Any implementation must contradict one of those statements, and an operator cannot tell whether an explicit gate order excludes the project default reviewers.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:6

chunk_findings.detail: The docs say “A reviewer with none of these runs as before, in addition to the chain,” while also saying “the first that answers is the review.” Given `[review].gate_order = {critic = "kimi,qwen"}` and another configured reviewer `codex` with no `priority`, no entry in `priority_default`, and no entry in `gate_order`, the docs say `codex` runs in addition to the ordered chain. If `codex` answers first, the “first that answers” sentence makes it the review, but it is outside the ordered failover chain and its skip/failover/independence semantics are undefined; if the chain answer is supposed to win, the “in addition to the chain” sentence is wrong. This makes the failover order non-deterministic for mixed configured gates.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:8

chunk_findings.detail: The docs describe the chain cooldown as only “one waits inside a single selection,” separate from `[review].degraded_cooldown_s`, which “prunes the pool across runs.” But the same document earlier says the chain cooldown is “remembered in `.ddflow/local/reviewer-cooldown.json`, so the next gate run skips it too.” If a reviewer returns 403 on gate A with `failover_cooldown_s` set, gate B will also skip it, so the chain cooldown does prune across runs just like the degraded cooldown. The claimed separation/tuning guidance is therefore wrong.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:20

chunk_findings.detail: The test is meant to cover the amendment’s family-independence rule, but it never supplies an author family and only asserts that the recorded answerer’s family is `anthropic`. If `run_chain` accepted an answer from a reviewer in the author’s family (e.g. author family `anthropic`, reviewer `a`/`google` unavailable, reviewer `b`/`anthropic` answers), this test would still pass, although the amendment requires the gate to stay unavailable when only the author’s family answers. The stated regression coverage for family independence is therefore absent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:test_only_authors_family_answers_keeps_family_on_answerer

chunk_findings.detail: `test_ordering_default_gate_and_field` locks the resolver to the wrong order. `rev()` defaults `priority=0`, so `gem` and `qwen` are 0 and `kimi` is 1, and `priority_default` is `["gem", "kimi", "qwen"]`. The amendment requires lower priority first and that list as the project order, which is `["gem", "qwen", "kimi"]` if the field is the sort key, or `["gem", "kimi", "qwen"]` if the default list is authoritative. The assertion demands `["kimi", "gem", "qwen"]`, so a resolver that follows either rule fails this test, and one that passes it tries the higher-priority reviewer before both the lower-priority peers and the configured default order.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:134

chunk_findings.detail: The new `priority_default` documentation says “Empty AND no reviewer has a `priority` field = no chain: every reviewer of the gate runs, as before.” That directly contradicts the same change’s `Reviewer.priority` comment at `ddflow/services/review/model.py:90`, which says a reviewer is placed by a name in `[review].priority_default` **or a per-gate order**, and contradicts the stated feature that a gate may carry an explicit ordered list. Given `[review].gate_order = {critic = "qwen,deepseek"}`, `[review].priority_default = []`, and no reviewer having a `priority` field, the doc claims there is no chain and all gate reviewers run, while the per-gate order is supposed to create a chain. Either the new contract is wrong, or `gate_order` is not participating in the chain as documented.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:98

chunk_findings.detail: The changed `except` clause catches `TypeError` but still lets `OverflowError` escape. If `.ddflow/local/reviewer-cooldown.json` is valid JSON but contains an integer too large for a C double, for example `{"kimi": 1` followed by 400 zeros and `}`, `json.loads` parses the value as an arbitrary-precision `int`; `float(v)` then raises `OverflowError`, which is not in the except tuple. That error propagates through `left`/`mark` and crashes `run_chain`, even though the cool-down loader is intended to treat bad cool-down data as “no memory” and continue.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_priority.py:CoolDowns._load

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentence “A reviewer in none of these is NOT in the try order for that gate” contradicts the unchanged contract in `tests/test_review_failover.py:test_ordering_default_gate_and_field`, which says “nothing prioritised: run-all as before” and asserts that with `priority_default=[]` and `gate_order={}`, un-prioritized reviewers are returned in `rest`. Given a project with configured reviewers but no `priority`, no `priority_default`, and no `gate_order`, the new docs say those reviewers are not tried, while the test’s stated behavior is that the gate still runs all reviewers as before. This makes the changed documentation misstate the gate’s try order for the no-priority configuration.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:12

chunk_findings.detail:
The rewritten spec says the chain is the whole try order, a `gate_order` entry replaces the default and only those names are tried, and a reviewer with no `priority`, no `priority_default` entry, and no `gate_order` entry is not tried. `tests/test_review_failover.py:153` still requires `RP.order([rev("p"), rev("q")], "critic", default=[], gate_order={})` to return `chain == []` and `rest` of length 2, commented “nothing prioritised: run-all as before”, and the preceding assertion still puts `gem` and `kimi` in `rest` rather than dropping them. Given reviewers `p` and `q` with no priority and empty default/gate_order, the locked resolver therefore still hands them back to be run, so the new “NOT in the try order” sentence is false for that input (and the same split applies when `gate_order` names only some reviewers).

Findings 1–3 cannot be verified from this part: the `run_chain` / `CoolDowns` edits are not in the diff shown.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:13

chunk_findings.detail: The new failover path invokes reviewers before the re-run refusal check can stop the gate. `run_reviewers` eagerly evaluates `pairs = [(r, one(r)) for r in rest]`, which calls `one` for every non-chain reviewer, and then `RP.run_chain` may call `one` for chain attempts; `run.py` only consults `_rerun_refusal` afterward. In the previous code, when `prior` was set and the first reviewer result was an ERROR or a non-matching cut, `_review_gate` returned `REFUSED` immediately and later reviewers were not invoked. Given a gate with a non-chain reviewer `A` that returns ERROR and a prioritized chain reviewer `B`, the new code still calls `B` (and possibly other chain attempts), creating `_ReplyFile` entries, issuing API requests, and potentially marking cooldowns, then returns `REFUSED` because of `A`. That is wrong because a refusal without recording should not consume later reviewers’ quota or mutate cooldown/reply-file state.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/failover.py:run_reviewers

chunk_findings.detail: `test_whole_chain_down_gate_gets_unavailable` does not actually prove that the priority chain was exhausted. It only checks that the final returned pair is unavailable and that `answered_by` is empty; it never records the calls or asserts that `ev["failover"]["attempts"]` contains both reviewers and their skip reasons. Given a `run_reviewers` implementation that treats `timeout` as terminal (or otherwise returns after the first unavailable reviewer), the test still passes: `a` returns `RV.UNAVAILABLE("timeout")`, `b` is never tried, `pairs` is still one unavailable result, and `answered_by` is `""`. That violates the amendment’s requirement that timeout is an unavailable condition and the next reviewer in priority is tried, with the reason for each skip recorded. The first test only covers HTTP 403, so the timeout failover path is not actually tested by this new gate test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover_gate.py:76

evidence.diff_source: delta review of 4 commits since aeb5633048

chunk_findings.detail: The new loop passes results produced by the failover chain to the existing `_note_degraded(... cfg.review.degraded_cooldown_s ...)` call. If a gate’s chain has one reviewer (or every reviewer in the chain fails) and that reviewer returns HTTP 403, `RP.run_chain` has already applied the failover cool-down (`failover_cooldown_s`, e.g. 300s) and returned the 403 result. The same result is then marked degraded for `degraded_cooldown_s` (e.g. 3600s). After the failover cool-down expires, the resolver would be willing to retry the reviewer, but the degraded mark still sheds it from its gate, so the amendment’s “skipped for a cool-down knob … retried after the cool-down, then returned to its place” does not happen. The documentation distinction between resolver failover and gate-pool degradation does not fix this because this code path applies both marks to the same 403 result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:_review_gate

chunk_findings.detail: For a rerun (`prior` true), `run_reviewers` sets `rest = list(revs)` and then immediately evaluates `pairs = [(r, one(r)) for r in rest]`, so every reviewer’s `one()` call (which creates a `_ReplyFile` and invokes `RV.review`) runs before `run.py` can check `_rerun_refusal`. Given `revs=[A, B]`, a non-empty `prior`, and `A` returning an ERROR, the new code still runs `B` and creates `B`’s reply-file side effects even though the original loop would have returned `REFUSED` after `A` without running `B`. This can consume reviewer quota and leave reply-file side effects for a review that is refused without recording.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/failover.py:run_reviewers

chunk_findings.detail: The new `gate_order` and `priority_default` knob docs give incompatible chain-membership rules for a gate that has an explicit order. Given `[review] gate_order = ["critic=a"]`, `[review] priority_default = []`, and a configured critic reviewer `b` with `priority = 1`, the `priority_default` doc says `b` “joins an ordered CHAIN when it has a `priority` field,” while the `gate_order` doc says “Only the named reviewers form the chain” for that gate. The operator cannot tell whether `b` is part of the critic failover chain or runs outside it; if the implementation follows `gate_order`, the `priority_default` membership rule is wrong for ordered gates, and if it follows `priority_default`, the explicit per-gate order is not authoritative.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:gate_order

chunk_findings.detail: The paragraph beginning “A reviewer with a `priority`...” still defines chain membership only by `priority` or `[review].priority_default`, without limiting it to the “otherwise” case introduced in the preceding bullet. Given `[review].gate_order.critic = ["lan"]` and a configured reviewer `lan` that has no `priority` and is not named in `priority_default`, lines 7–9 say `lan` “IS the chain for that gate” and “only the named reviewers form the chain,” while line 13 says a reviewer with none of these is “not part of the chain itself” and falls to `rest`. An operator following line 13 would conclude the explicit per-gate chain does not exist and the un-prioritised `lan` runs as before, contradicting the documented `gate_order` behavior required by the amendment. The doc must say this membership rule applies only when no `gate_order` entry exists, or otherwise clarify that `gate_order` names are chain members regardless of `priority`/`priority_default`.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:13
